Any unprivileged local user can make the NetBird daemon read arbitrary files as root.

The daemon socket at `/var/run/netbird.sock` accepts unauthenticated local requests. By setting an arbitrary path through `RegisterUILog` and then requesting a debug bundle, an attacker can cause the root-privileged daemon to include that file in the bundle and upload it to an attacker-controlled loopback endpoint.

### Details

The issue is probably caused by the interaction between `RegisterUILog` and `DebugBundle`.

`RegisterUILog` accepts a caller-controlled filesystem path without restricting it to a legitimate NetBird log file. `DebugBundle` later opens that path using the daemon’s privileges and adds its contents to the generated archive.

The caller also controls the bundle upload endpoint. As a result, an unprivileged local process can point the UI log path at a root-only file, request a bundle, and receive the file contents over e.g. `127.0.0.1`.

No NetBird account, administrative privileges, user interaction, or external network access are required.

### Impact

This is a local arbitrary file-read vulnerability in a root-privileged service.

Any unprivileged user or compromised local process on an affected system may be able to read files accessible to the NetBird daemon, including password hashes, private keys, service credentials, authentication material, and data belonging to other users.

The issue breaks the local operating-system privilege boundary and may expose credentials that enable further local or remote compromise.

### Fix

Fixed in 0.76.1 ([#6975](https://github.com/netbirdio/netbird/pull/6975)). Three changes close the chain:

- `RegisterUILog` now requires a caller the daemon can identify from the control channel, and accepts only an absolute local path whose file name is the UI log's. UNC and device paths are refused, so the root daemon cannot be pointed at a remote or device namespace.
- The bundle opens the UI log as the requesting user rather than as root, so a caller only ever collects a file it already owns. A caller whose identity cannot be established gets no UI log in the bundle at all.
- The upload destination is restricted. NetBird's public upload service stays open to any caller, since the CLI and the desktop UI use it, but any other endpoint, and any relaxed transport security, requires a privileged caller.

### Affected platforms

Desktop clients on Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD. The Android and iOS apps are not affected: they embed the client engine directly and never expose the daemon control socket the attack requires.

### Credits

Security research and disclosure by Frederick Stempfle on behalf of Whitelisthackers.
